x.A: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections, so bursts of serverless connections don't exceed the database's limit. Applications only need to point at the proxy.
x.B: A Memcached cache reduces read queries but doesn't pool connections, and writes still open connections, plus it needs application changes.
x.C: A higher I/O instance class doesn't fix the number of connections the database can accept.
x.D: Multi-AZ gives failover, but the standby isn't used for connections, and switching between instances in the application is manual.

x.A: A scheduled Lambda function running remote scripts isn't tied to launch and terminate events, so instances might launch or terminate between runs without reporting.
x.B: Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks pause the instance at launch and termination so a custom script can send the data before the instance proceeds. Every instance reports at both points.
x.C: User data runs only at launch, so it doesn't report at termination, and a launch configuration can't run anything when the instance is terminated.
x.D: A script invoked by the instance itself isn't triggered by the Auto Scaling group at termination, so it can't be relied on to run.

x.A: Route 53 distributes traffic by DNS and doesn't handle UDP traffic like a load balancer, and Aurora Serverless is relational, which isn't needed for non-relational data.
x.B: A Network Load Balancer supports UDP, and DynamoDB on-demand scales for non-relational data such as scores without any intervention.
x.C: Aurora Global Database is a relational database for cross-Region replication, which doesn't fit non-relational data and costs more.
x.D: An ALB doesn't support UDP, and global tables are meant for multi-Region replication, which isn't needed.

x.A: Letting the frontend connect directly to the database bypasses the API, which is insecure and changes the architecture.
x.B: Provisioned concurrency keeps Lambda environments initialized with the libraries loaded, so requests avoid cold start delays. It needs only a configuration change.
x.C: Caching query results in S3 isn't faster than the database for this use, and it needs code changes.
x.D: A bigger database allows more connections but doesn't fix the cold start time from loading libraries.

x.A: EC2 instances can't be scaled with elastic resize (that's a Redshift feature), and RDS instances can't be scaled to zero.
x.B: Marketplace partner solutions add cost and require evaluation, setup, and licensing, so they aren't the lowest cost.
x.C: Another EC2 instance running a crontab adds a server to pay for and maintain.
x.D: A Lambda function that starts and stops the instances, invoked on a schedule by EventBridge, is serverless, cheap, and needs little maintenance.

x.A: DocumentDB is a different database, and moving from PostgreSQL would need significant application changes.
x.B: Aurora PostgreSQL is compatible with PostgreSQL, so the code changes are minimal. An Aurora Replica serves the long-running reports so document writes on the primary are not affected.
x.C: The standby in an RDS Multi-AZ deployment can't be queried, so reporting can't run against the secondary node.
x.D: DynamoDB is a different data model and doesn't support relational queries, so it would need major code changes.

x.A: A TLS listener on the NLB with the server certificate encrypts traffic between devices and the load balancer, which improves the security of the data in transit.
x.B: Shield Advanced and WAF protect against attacks, and WAF doesn't work with an NLB. They don't encrypt data in transit.
x.C: Changing to an ALB with WAF filters web attacks but doesn't by itself secure the sensor data in transit.
x.D: Encrypting EBS volumes protects data at rest, not data in transit.

x.A: A Dedicated Host gives visibility of sockets and cores for licensing with existing licenses, and Reserved pricing is cheaper for predictable, steady usage than On-Demand.
x.B: Dedicated On-Demand Hosts cost more than reserved hosts for a predictable, constant workload.
x.C: Dedicated Instances don't give visibility into sockets and cores, so they can't be used for socket-based licenses.
x.D: Dedicated On-Demand Instances also don't give socket and core visibility and cost more.

x.A: S3 isn't POSIX-compliant, and Glacier isn't suited to frequently accessed shared data.
x.B: S3 isn't a POSIX-compliant file system that can be mounted and shared across instances in the same way.
x.C: EFS Standard is POSIX-compliant, stores data across multiple AZs for maximum durability, and can be shared across instances. A lifecycle policy moves infrequently accessed files to EFS Standard-IA to save cost.
x.D: EFS One Zone stores data in a single AZ, which gives less durability and availability than required.

x.A: Allowing port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on the web servers opens them to anywhere, which is more than they need. They only need traffic from the load balancer.
x.B: A network ACL can't reference a security group, and ACLs are stateless and broader, so this isn't a valid least-privilege approach.
x.C: The web server security group allows 443 only from the load balancer's security group, and the MySQL security group allows 3306 only from the web servers' security group. Each tier gets only the access it needs.
x.D: Network ACLs can't reference security groups, so the rules aren't valid.

x.A: SNS is a notification service and doesn't store or return database results.
x.B: ElastiCache caches frequently requested, identical datasets in memory, so the backend avoids repeated database calls and performance improves.
x.C: A read replica adds read capacity but isn't a cache, and identical queries still hit a database each time.
x.D: Firehose streams data to destinations and doesn't cache database calls.

x.A: The root user has unrestricted access, so using it for daily work breaks least privilege and is bad practice.
x.B: PowerUser access gives broad permissions across most services, far more than CloudFormation work needs.
x.C: AdministratorAccess gives full access, which isn't least privilege.
x.D: An IAM user in a group with a policy that allows CloudFormation actions only limits what the engineer can do directly.
x.E: A role that explicitly defines the permissions for the CloudFormation stack, which CloudFormation assumes when launching stacks, keeps permissions specific and temporary.

x.A: The default network ACL already allows all traffic, so adding an explicit rule isn't the problem.
x.B: The VPC's local route already allows traffic between subnets in the VPC, so no route needs to be added.
x.C: Putting them in separate VPCs adds complexity and isn't needed, because they're already in the same VPC.
x.D: The database's security group in its default state doesn't allow inbound traffic from the web tier. Adding an inbound rule from the web tier's security group lets the application connect.

x.A: A read replica handles the reporting queries separately, so they don't affect writes on the production instance.
x.B: A load balancer doesn't distribute traffic across database writes, and you can't scale out a single RDS instance horizontally that way.
x.C: A larger instance still runs queries and writes on the same database, so reports can still slow down writes.
x.D: The standby in a Multi-AZ deployment can't be used for queries, so it doesn't offload reports.

x.A: Sticky sessions keep a user on one instance, but the session data is lost if the instance fails, so it isn't durable.
x.B: DynamoDB stores the session data durably and scales, and any instance can read it, which suits session management.
x.C: A Cognito user pool manages users and authentication, but it isn't a store for application session data during transactions.
x.D: ElastiCache for Redis stores session data in memory with replication and persistence options, so any instance can access it, and it's fast.
x.E: Systems Manager Application Manager is for managing application resources, not for storing user session data.

x.A: Snapshots of the instances' EBS volumes every 2 hours back up stateless instances that don't need it, wasting resources and not improving scalability.
x.B: EBS snapshots of the stateless instances aren't needed, and a lifecycle policy for them wastes resources.
x.C: The web tier is stateless, so keeping the latest AMIs is enough to recreate it. RDS automated backups with point-in-time recovery meet the 2 hour RPO for the database.
x.D: Taking EBS snapshots of the stateless instances is unnecessary and wastes resources.

x.A: The web servers must accept HTTPS from customers with dynamic IP addresses, so 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 is needed. The database accepts port 3306 only from the web servers' security group, keeping it private.
x.B: Customers have dynamic IP addresses, so you can't list their IPs in the security group.
x.C: This also lists customer IPs, which can't be known, and it would expose the database to customers.
x.D: Allowing the database to accept connections from 0.0.0.0/0 exposes it to the internet, which isn't secure.

x.A: Kinesis Video Streams handles video streams, and scanning with Lambda for known patterns isn't a proper transcription and redaction.
x.B: Textract extracts text from documents and images, not from audio recordings.
x.C: Transcribe converts audio to text and has a built-in option to redact PII from the transcript. A Lambda function can start the job on upload, and the redacted output goes to a separate bucket.
x.D: Amazon Connect is a contact center service and isn't meant for processing recordings from S3, and the Lambda PII scan needs custom code.

x.A: Magnetic volumes provide far fewer IOPS than gp3, so performance would be worse.
x.B: gp3 volumes are limited to 16,000 IOPS, so you can't raise it beyond that to cover more than 20,000.
x.C: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) supports far higher IOPS, so the database can handle more than 20,000 read and write IOPS during peak demand.
x.D: RDS doesn't let you stripe two gp3 volumes in place of one that way, and the IOPS limit per volume remains.

x.A: GuardDuty detects threats and anomalies and doesn't give a record of who made a specific change.
x.B: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and doesn't record who changed configuration.
x.C: CloudTrail records API calls, including who made them and when, so it shows which IAM user changed the security group rules.
x.D: AWS Config records what a resource's configuration was and how it changed, but it doesn't identify which user made the change as directly as CloudTrail.

x.A: Shield Advanced can protect a Global Accelerator accelerator directly, so adding the accelerator as a protected resource covers the DNS solution against DDoS attacks.
x.B: The EC2 instances are behind the accelerator and Shield Advanced protection should be on the accelerator, which is the internet-facing resource.
x.C: WAF can't be associated with a Global Accelerator accelerator, and rate-based rules apply to HTTP traffic.
x.D: WAF can't be associated with EC2 instances, and a DNS service isn't HTTP traffic.

x.A: Lambda has a 15 minute limit, so a job that takes up to an hour can't run there.
x.B: The same Lambda time limit applies, and API Gateway adds an unneeded component.
x.C: An ECS task on Fargate runs the job without servers to manage for as long as it needs, triggered by an EventBridge schedule. It handles the large objects and an hour of runtime with the least effort.
x.D: ECS on EC2 needs you to manage an EC2 instance and Auto Scaling group, so it has more operational work.

x.A: At 100 Mbps, 600 TB would take years to upload, so S3 multipart upload over HTTPS can't finish in 2 weeks.
x.B: A VPN uses the same internet connection and is just as slow.
x.C: Several Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices can carry 600 TB offline and encrypt the data in transit, so the transfer completes within 2 weeks at a reasonable cost.
x.D: Direct Connect takes weeks to set up and costs more than Snowball devices for a one-time transfer.

x.A: CloudFront caching for 24 hours would serve stale stock prices, and it doesn't stop an HTTP flood by itself.
x.B: A Regional AWS WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule blocks IP addresses that send too many requests, which protects the API from HTTP floods, and it attaches directly to the API Gateway stage.
x.C: Monitoring and alerting only notifies the team, and doesn't block attacks.
x.D: Lambda@Edge with a custom blocking function means building and maintaining code, which WAF does with a rule.

x.A: DynamoDB transactions group reads and writes and can't notify teams.
x.B: Having the application publish to four topics changes the application and can slow it down, which the company wants to avoid.
x.C: DynamoDB Streams captures new items and triggers a Lambda function that publishes to one SNS topic the teams subscribe to. The current application isn't affected and nothing needs to be polled.
x.D: A cron job that scans the table every minute adds read load on the table and more infrastructure to maintain.
